dqtr.text: Translation of the quoted passage: Apart from the accent of individual words, the accent of speech deserves attention, which serves to emphasize the main concepts, whole sentences, giving them a varied shade of meaning. This accent of speech, or of the sentence, surpasses the word accent in duration, expiratory force and height of tone.

1851.dq: Prócz akcentu poszczególnych wyrazów zasługuje na uwagę akcent mowy, który służy do podkreślania głównych pojęć, całych zdań, nadając im rozmaity odcień znaczeniowy. Ten akcent mowy czy zdania przewyższa trwaniem, siłą ekspiracyjną i wysokością tonu akcent wyrazowy.
1851.dloc: Kleczkowski 1920, ch. II, section 'Ogólna podstawa artykulacji wil.' (pp. 28-29): p. 29, last paragraph before 'III. Fonetyka' (archive.org pracepolska01pols scan, slice); word accent (akcent wyrazowy) explicitly distinguished from speech/sentence accent (akcent mowy czy zdania).
1851.prule: Native (German-stock) words keep the inherited German accent placement 'well and without any fluctuation' (Kleczkowski 1920 p. 23): the expiratory stress 'traditionally, as in German, rests in German words mostly on the first [syllable]' and 'almost always agrees with the value-stress (Wertdruck)', rarely yielding to rhythmic or unit stress (c. p. 29), i.e. stem/root stress; verbal prefixes by-, cy- (and participial gy-) are unaccented per Andrason & Krol 2016; in trisyllables prominence decays with distance from the main stress; compounds carry strengthened main stress on the first member with reduction of the second. (Kleczkowski's remark 'vor- = fer- nieakcentowane, fir- akcentowane' concerns the Schoenwald sister dialect, not Wilamowice.)
1851.srule: Only in compounds: simplex words carry one stress (in trisyllables the post-tonic syllables weaken steadily with distance from the main stress, no rhythmic secondary, Kleczkowski 1920 p. 25); a secondary accent (akcent poboczny) is noted only on the second member of compounds and on heavy compound-like suffixes (-heit, -weiz), where it is mostly weakened with vowel shortening (§103 p. 85, §192 p. 133).

1852.heavy: Vowel 'durch Natur oder Position lang' (long by nature or by position, i.e. long vowel or vowel in a closed syllable); in disyllables the final wins if its vowel outweighs the penult's in quantity, and a short vowel in a closed final syllable outweighs a short vowel in an open penult; a (also ạ) derived from an older long ā counts as long for accent (Anmerkung to d).
1852.dflt: not stated (norms b-d cover unequal quantity and long penult only; light-light disyllables not addressed)
1852.prule: Reinisch 1884 par. 83 (Chamir of Soqota/Lasta and Wag, i.e. the Seqot'a variety of Xamtanga; hedged as general norms after admitting inconsistent accent marking in his own notes): main accent never on the antepenult, only on the final or the penult; (b) disyllables: final accent when the final vowel outweighs the penult vowel in quantity; (c) a short vowel in a (singly or doubly) closed final syllable outweighs a short vowel in a preceding open syllable; (d) penult accent when the penult vowel is long by nature or by position; (e) trisyllables follow b-d, with a secondary accent on the antepenult when the final carries the main accent. Hetzron 1976:12 restates it as 'In Xamir, stress falls on one of the last two syllables, conditioned by vowel quality.'
1852.srule: Reinisch 1884 par. 83 e: in trisyllabic words with final main accent the antepenult (initial) syllable gets a secondary accent ('zugleich erhält die drittletzte Silbe einen Nebenaccent, wenn die letzte Silbe den Hauptton trägt', e.g. birberä, digürä); no secondary accent mentioned for penult-accented words; words of four or more syllables not addressed. Later sources reached (Hetzron 1976, Teshome 2015, Mous 2021 carrying Darmon 2015) say nothing about secondary stress.

1860.dq: Each word has one, and only one, stress syllable. (Renck 1967:42); Stress, i.e. the main word stress, is indicated in the Yagaria Dictionary by the accent (Renck 1975:15); But since that word has two stresses, it is treated as two separate words in the phonemic spelling (Renck 1975:14).

1860.prule: Stress is phonemic (emic): contrasts in analogous environments, minimal pairs distinguished by stress alone ('havu 'root' vs ha'vu 'bow'; 'gaena 'line' vs ga'ena); main stress may fall word-initially, medially or finally; each word has exactly one main stress; no positional or weight rule is stated. Three degrees (stress / non-stress / reduced); certain prefixes (ma-, na-) always unstressed or reduced.
1860.quote: [Renck 1975 sec. 1.1.3] Three tones may be observed in Yagaria, low, mid, and high. But only two minimal word pairs have been discovered which contrast by mid and low tones, so that the existence of two tonemes may be stated: /'ve/ 'man', /'ve/ 'spirit', /ha'li/ 'fire', /ha'li/ 'arrow'. But this basis obviously is too narrow to establish Yagaria as a tone language. In all other cases where the occurrence of minimal pairs depends on suprasegments, stress is the decisive factor, and the occurring tone is closely linked with stress: /'havu/ 'root', /ha'vu/ 'bow', /'gaena/ 'line', /ga'ena/ 'penis…

1861.prule: Khromov 1972 (synchronic): NOUNS - stress falls either on the final syllable or, 'most often', on the penult (vurúk, sirísp vs ɣúrda, kátta, mákša); no conditioning stated for the choice; Tajik loans take penult stress in Yaghnobi speech (hamsóya) vs final in Tajik. COMPOUNDS - main stress on the first member if it contains a long vowel, secondary on the second. VERBS - stress on the stem vowel if it is long (§26); if the stem vowel is short, in finite forms (except aorist) stress moves to the ending vowel if that is long (except 1sg pres.-fut. -omišt), stays on the stem vowel if the ending vowel is short, and stays on a short stem vowel closed by two consonants regardless of the ending (§27); aorist of short-vowel stems: stress always on the ending (§28); participles -ta/-na and converb -ki: stress on stem vowel (§29); participle -gi: stress word-final (§30); negative forms: main stress always on the negation particle na- (§31). Always unstressed: enclitic pronouns, oblique -i, possessive -ik, distributive -ki (§25). Novák 2013 (diachronic): Yaghnobi stress position continues Proto-Sogdic 'Stress II' = penult if it held a long vowel or a short vowel/diphthong in a closed syllable, else antepenult (Latin-type), with later loss of post-tonic vowels; 'Yaghnōbī retained original stress on (ante)penultima (i.e. Stress II)'.

morph.elicq: The stress section (Khromov 1972 §§22-31) cites only isolated word forms with accent marks and does not say how stress was determined. The only methodological statement is the general one for the whole grammar (p.10): 'Материал был собран путем полевых записей во время нескольких экспедиций в долину р. Ягноб ... Живя в ягнобских семьях, мы имели возможность записывать непринужденную речь ягнобцев. Сбор материалов производился путем записи на магнитофонную ленту, которая затем расшифровывалась в лабораторных условиях, и путем записи на слух.'…
morph.stmt: Predominantly suffixing and agglutinating: 'Yaghnobi nouns only take suffixes; they do not take prefixes or infixes' (Bird 2007 p.25 fn.2) and 'The morphology of the Yaghnobi language is agglutinating and, to a limited degree, polysynthetic' (p.14); the verb carries person/number, tense (-iʃt), participial and nominalising suffixes plus pronominal enclitics, with exactly two pre-root elements -- the past-tense augment a- ('past tense is signaled by the prefix a-', Bird p.76; Khromov §80) and the negative na- -- and Khromov §297 notes bar-dih- as 'единственный приставочный глагол в ягнобском языке' (the only prefixed verb in the language).

1862.dq: Section is titled 'Word stress and stress shift': 'Primary stress is predictable and always occurs on the penultimate syllable of the word.' 1862.prule: Primary stress fixed on the penultimate syllable of the word (quantity-insensitive, stated without hedge); one secondary stress on the second syllable to the left of the primary in words of more than three syllables (a single secondary, not described as iterating); monosyllables carry weak stress; suffixation (incl. enclitic pronoun -ku) shifts stress one syllable rightward so that it stays penultimate.
1862.srule: In words of more than three syllables, one secondary stress on the second syllable to the left of the penultimate primary (4-syl 2010, 5-syl 02010; Behrens 1975 p. 14 transcribes /"ma.ka.'ja.di/, /ma."mag.qa.'ka.hin/); 2-3-syllable words have no secondary; described as a single secondary, iteration in words longer than five syllables not described.

Syllables with neither primary nor secondary stress, including monosyllabic words, carry weak stress. Primary stress is predictable and always occurs on the penultimate syllable of the word. One phrase-level remark in §2.5 (9): "The change of a to e also occurs across word boundaries within a phrase if primary phrase stress overrides primary word stress ("a'a "bahi' mi"ya'an -> e'e behi' mi"ya'an 'that old person')."
morph.stmt: Yakan is mixed but verb-prefixing/noun-suffixing: verbs take voice, mood and derivational prefixes and the infix -in- (mag-, N-, pa-, ta-, maka-, paN-; "if mag- or N- is added to the root, it becomes the verb magsumping or numping"), nominalisation uses circumfixes (ka-…-an, pag-…-an, mag-…-in), while post-root material is the definite suffix -in, applicative -an, imperative -un and the bound ergative/genitive pronouns ("Ergative and genitive pronouns... are phonologically bound forms", §3.5.1), all of which sit inside the penultimate-stress word ("Suffixation causes stress to shift one syllable to the right", §2.4); case, plural, aspect, negation and question marking are free particles.

tn.translation: As a complement we briefly recall the vowel and tone systems, which have undergone no modification: ... TONES Simple L: v̀ M: v̄ H: v́ Modulated Rising L.M: v̀v̄ L.H: v̀v́ (M.H: v̄v́) Falling M.L: v̄v̀ H.L: v́v̀ ... The modulated tone M-H represents a dialectal (?) variant of the high tone in certain cases ... [Rule 1] - its tone combines with the tone of the final vowel of the preceding word and is realised as a complex modulation. It is assimilated to it when it is identical to the tone, or to the last mora (if that tone is modulated), of the final vowel of the preceding word.

1865.dq: The label 'phrase stress' is used in preference to 'sentence stress' for a strong stress which appears on at least one syllable in most sentences ... The position of the phrase stress is unpredictable; it may even appear on a syllable that would not normally carry any word stress
1865.dloc: Ch.3 sec.3.6 'Stress', pp.30-32 (of OAPEN/ANU eView; running heads 'Pronunciation 31', '32 Chapter 3'); sec.3.6.1 'Phrase stress', p.33
1865.prule: Primary stress on the first syllable of any word (quantity-insensitive, fixed initial).
1865.srule: Secondary stress on the third syllable of a four-syllable root or of a trisyllabic word plus monosyllabic suffix (thálkapàrlu; tjúkurru-li ~ tjúkurrù-li), on the first syllable of any bound disyllabic morpheme (máka-mùdu-li, yándha-yàndha-rnànga), and on the first of a pair of bound monosyllabic suffixes unless it is -yi after /a/,/i/ (kárrpa-ngà-la-tji; alternatively on a monosyllabic suffix preceding a disyllabic one, -nà-rnanga ~ -na-rnànga); gerund -ini/-ni does not count as disyllabic; syllable deletion or coalescence can leave a secondary right after the primary ([yákàkaŋa], [ŋálàːku]). 1866.dflt: Not stated as such; strength is relative (rule 2: ma'pa -> [má'pa], V' beats V); for equal final/penult the penult wins (rule 4); no explicit statement for longer all-(C)V words

1871.prule: No phonemic stress. 1872.dq: Na língua Yawalapiti, observamos que o acento de intensidade incide na última e penúltima sílaba fonética da palavra.
1872.dloc: Part I sec. 3.1 'Acento' p.25; sec. 6 'Acento' pp.38-39; sec. 7 'Duração' p.40; Part II note 9
1872.prule: Word stress (acento tônico / de intensidade) is phonemic (contrastive), restricted to the last two syllables of the word: it falls on either the final or the penultimate syllable, unpredictably, with minimal pairs (pi'ti 'bury' vs 'piti 'village'; pa'wa 'one' vs 'pawa 'other'). Patterns with stress further left are 'not permitted by the language'.
1872.srule: Not mentioned in Mujica 1992 (Part I secs. 3.1, 6, 7 'Acento'/'Duração', pp.25, 38-40, and Notas pp.68-69 read): only one stress per word is marked and no secondary or rhythmic stress is discussed. (Tapi Yawalapíti 2021 sec. 2.8, pp.91-93, likewise gives no secondary-stress statement.)

dfl.note: Mujica 1992 states only that phonemic stress falls on the final or the penultimate syllable and gives minimal pairs; no default or majority position is stated (secs. 3.1, 6, 7 read in full). Tapi 2021 p.91 says explicitly that the accent cannot be called predictable, since morphologically unsegmentable words split between penultimate and final accent, and lists 7 penult-accented and 16 final-accented roots (pp.91-92) without calling either the majority.

1875.prule: Word stress falls on the first (leftmost) syllable containing the low open vowel /a/; if the word has no /a/, stress is initial. The 1973 primary states the two rules in this order (rule 2 explicitly the elsewhere case) and gives stress-marked examples: [sɨ'ᵽa] 'seed', [wɒ'ramsɨ] 'tobacco' (stress skips an initial /ɨ/ or /ɔ/ syllable to reach /a/), ['amʌᵐbʌ] 'running', ['tʰɨtɨtɨ] 'will stand', ['lowsɨ] 'tongs' (no /a/ -> initial). The 1973 vowel inventory is /ɨ ʌ ɔ a/ (p.80), so the conditioner is one specific vowel quality (the lowest, most sonorous vowel) against all others including back /ɔ/; not syllable weight: no length contrast, codas play no role (['lowsɨ], ['tʰowk'naᵐbʌ]).

1877.tone: Michaud classes Na with Mandarin and Yoruba as a language whose lexically distinctive prosodic property is tone (not stress, not tonal accent). Three levels H/M/L, tone group as the domain of tone rules; H is culminative within the tone group and post-H levelling is explicitly compared to post-stress de-stressing, but the author analyses it as tone, contrasting Na with 'terracing' tone languages rather than reanalysing it as accent. The only 'stress' in the book is emphatic stress = focus/pragmatic intonation (§8.3.1), described as a near-universal and not lexical. No statement of a default word-stress position; the book never asserts 'Na has no word stress' in so many words, but its prosodic taxonomy (§8.1.1) assigns Na tone where English has stress.

tn.quote: There are three tonal levels in Yongning Na, H(igh), M(id) and L(ow). The tone-bearing unit is the syllable, more specifically the syllable rhyme. ... any syllable rhyme, including syllabic consonants, can function as a tone-bearing unit for one or two tonal levels. Out of six theoretically possible contours (HM, HL, MH, ML, LH, and LM), only the three rising contours (MH, LH and LM) are attested as lexical categories ... each syllable within a tone group carries one of three levels: H, M or L, and the last syllable can carry one of the following: H, M, L, MH, or LH.
tn.cite: Michaud, Alexis. 2017. Tone in Yongning Na: Lexical tones and morphotonology (Studies in Diversity Linguistics 13). Berlin: Language Science Press.
tn.note: Three level tones H/M/L on the syllable rhyme; rising contours MH/LH/LM are level sequences confined to tone-group-final position; a floating H category; H culminative per tone group; no downstep. Checked against the source (tone consistency check, 2026-09-23): evidence elicitation -> instrumental (§8.1 Fig. 8.1 pp.358-359; §8.3.2 p.378).

corr.words: Figure 8.1: Spectrogram and F0 tracing of ‘pig’s brains’ and ‘is (a/the) pig’s brains’. Average fundamental frequency over the vowel /i/ in /li˩/ is two semitones lower than over the vowel /ĩ/ in the preceding syllable, /hĩ˧/ (210 Hz vs. 237 Hz), a phonetic difference that is in keeping with the phonological tones (M vs. L).
